Points

Distance

d=(x2−x1)2+(y2−y1)2d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}d=(x2​−x1​)2+(y2​−y1​)2​

Symbols: (x1,y1)(x_1, y_1)(x1​,y1​) and (x2,y2)(x_2, y_2)(x2​,y2​): the two points; ddd: the distance between them.

The idea

Draw the right triangle with horizontal side Δx\Delta xΔx and vertical side Δy\Delta yΔy; the segment is its hypotenuse, so Pythagoras gives its length. The order of the points does not matter because the differences are squared.

Worked example

A(1,2)A(1, 2)A(1,2), B(4,6)B(4, 6)B(4,6): Δx=3\Delta x = 3Δx=3, Δy=4\Delta y = 4Δy=4, so AB=9+16=5AB = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5AB=9+16​=5.

Midpoint

M=(x1+x22,y1+y22)M = \left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)M=(2x1​+x2​​,2y1​+y2​​)

Symbols: MMM: the midpoint of the segment from (x1,y1)(x_1, y_1)(x1​,y1​) to (x2,y2)(x_2, y_2)(x2​,y2​).

The idea

The midpoint is halfway in each direction: average the xxx-coordinates and average the yyy-coordinates. It is also how you find a missing endpoint: B=2M−AB = 2M - AB=2M−A.

Worked example

A(2,−1)A(2, -1)A(2,−1), B(6,5)B(6, 5)B(6,5): M=(82,42)=(4,2)M = \left(\tfrac{8}{2}, \tfrac{4}{2}\right) = (4, 2)M=(28​,24​)=(4,2).

Dividing in a ratio m : n

P=(nx1+mx2m+n,ny1+my2m+n)P = \left(\frac{n x_1 + m x_2}{m + n}, \frac{n y_1 + m y_2}{m + n}\right)P=(m+nnx1​+mx2​​,m+nny1​+my2​​)

Symbols: PPP lies on the segment from (x1,y1)(x_1, y_1)(x1​,y1​) to (x2,y2)(x_2, y_2)(x2​,y2​) with distances in the ratio m:nm : nm:n.

The idea

PPP divides ABABAB so that AP:PB=m:nAP : PB = m : nAP:PB=m:n. It is a weighted average where each endpoint is weighted by the share on the other side: BBB gets weight mmm, AAA gets nnn. Equivalently P=A+mm+n(B−A)P = A + \tfrac{m}{m + n}(B - A)P=A+m+nm​(B−A).

Worked example

A(1,2)A(1, 2)A(1,2), B(7,5)B(7, 5)B(7,5), AP:PB=1:2AP : PB = 1 : 2AP:PB=1:2: P=(2⋅1+1⋅73,2⋅2+1⋅53)=(3,3)P = \left(\tfrac{2\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 7}{3}, \tfrac{2\cdot 2 + 1\cdot 5}{3}\right) = (3, 3)P=(32⋅1+1⋅7​,32⋅2+1⋅5​)=(3,3) — one third of the way from AAA.

Centroid of a triangle

G=(x1+x2+x33,y1+y2+y33)G = \left(\frac{x_1 + x_2 + x_3}{3}, \frac{y_1 + y_2 + y_3}{3}\right)G=(3x1​+x2​+x3​​,3y1​+y2​+y3​​)

Symbols: (xi,yi)(x_i, y_i)(xi​,yi​): the three vertices; GGG: the centroid (where the medians meet).

The idea

The three medians meet at the centroid GGG, which is simply the average of the three vertices. It divides every median in the ratio 2:12 : 12:1 from the vertex — and it is where a cardboard triangle balances.

Worked example

Vertices (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0), (6,0)(6, 0)(6,0), (3,6)(3, 6)(3,6): G=(93,63)=(3,2)G = \left(\tfrac{9}{3}, \tfrac{6}{3}\right) = (3, 2)G=(39​,36​)=(3,2), one third of the height above the base.

Triangle area

S=12∣x1(y2−y3)+x2(y3−y1)+x3(y1−y2)∣S = \tfrac12\left|x_1(y_2 - y_3) + x_2(y_3 - y_1) + x_3(y_1 - y_2)\right|S=21​∣x1​(y2​−y3​)+x2​(y3​−y1​)+x3​(y1​−y2​)∣

Symbols: (x1,y1)(x_1, y_1)(x1​,y1​), (x2,y2)(x_2, y_2)(x2​,y2​), (x3,y3)(x_3, y_3)(x3​,y3​): the vertices; SSS: the area.

The idea

The “shoelace” formula gives the area straight from the coordinates, with no heights to find. The sign of the bracket tells the orientation (counter-clockwise positive), so take the absolute value. If it is 0, the points are collinear.

Worked example

(0,0)(0, 0)(0,0), (4,0)(4, 0)(4,0), (1,3)(1, 3)(1,3): 12∣0+4(3−0)+1(0−0)∣=6\tfrac12\lvert 0 + 4(3 - 0) + 1(0 - 0)\rvert = 621​∣0+4(3−0)+1(0−0)∣=6 — the same as base 4 × height 3 ÷ 2.

Distance in space

d=Δx2+Δy2+Δz2d = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + \Delta z^2}d=Δx2+Δy2+Δz2​

Symbols: Δx=x2−x1\Delta x = x_2 - x_1Δx=x2​−x1​, Δy=y2−y1\Delta y = y_2 - y_1Δy=y2​−y1​, Δz=z2−z1\Delta z = z_2 - z_1Δz=z2​−z1​: the differences of the coordinates.

The idea

In three dimensions apply Pythagoras twice: first across the floor (Δx\Delta xΔx, Δy\Delta yΔy), then up (Δz\Delta zΔz). The result is one more square under the root.

Worked example

(1,2,3)(1, 2, 3)(1,2,3) to (3,5,9)(3, 5, 9)(3,5,9): 4+9+36=49=7\sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = \sqrt{49} = 74+9+36​=49​=7.

Lines

Slope

m=y2−y1x2−x1=tan⁡αm = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} = \tan\alpham=x2​−x1​y2​−y1​​=tanα

Symbols: mmm: the slope; α\alphaα: the angle the line makes with the positive xxx-axis.

The idea

The slope is “rise over run”: how much yyy changes when xxx increases by 1. It equals tan⁡α\tan\alphatanα, where α\alphaα is the angle with the positive xxx-axis. Vertical lines have no slope.

Worked example

Through (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1) and (4,7)(4, 7)(4,7): m=63=2m = \tfrac{6}{3} = 2m=36​=2, so the angle is α=arctan⁡2≈63.4°\alpha = \arctan 2 \approx 63.4°α=arctan2≈63.4°.

Forms of a line

y=mx+by = mx + by=mx+by−y1=m(x−x1)y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)y−y1​=m(x−x1​)Ax+By+C=0Ax + By + C = 0Ax+By+C=0

Symbols: mmm: slope, bbb: yyy-intercept (where it cuts the yyy-axis), (x1,y1)(x_1, y_1)(x1​,y1​): a point of the line; A,B,CA, B, CA,B,C: numbers.

The idea

Slope–intercept y=mx+by = mx + by=mx+b is best for drawing; point–slope y−y1=m(x−x1)y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)y−y1​=m(x−x1​) is best when you know a point and the slope; the general form Ax+By+C=0Ax + By + C = 0Ax+By+C=0 also covers vertical lines and is what the distance formula uses.

Worked example

Through (2,3)(2, 3)(2,3) with slope −1-1−1: y−3=−(x−2)y - 3 = -(x - 2)y−3=−(x−2), i.e. y=−x+5y = -x + 5y=−x+5, or x+y−5=0x + y - 5 = 0x+y−5=0.

Intercept form

xa+yb=1\frac xa + \frac yb = 1ax​+by​=1

Symbols: aaa, bbb: where the line cuts the axes, at (a,0)(a, 0)(a,0) and (0,b)(0, b)(0,b).

The idea

If a line cuts the axes at (a,0)(a, 0)(a,0) and (0,b)(0, b)(0,b), its equation is xa+yb=1\tfrac xa + \tfrac yb = 1ax​+by​=1: put y=0y = 0y=0 and you get x=ax = ax=a. To read the intercepts from Ax+By=CAx + By = CAx+By=C, divide by CCC.

Worked example

x4+y2=1\tfrac x4 + \tfrac y2 = 14x​+2y​=1 meets the axes at (4,0)(4, 0)(4,0) and (0,2)(0, 2)(0,2); multiplying by 4 gives x+2y=4x + 2y = 4x+2y=4.

Parallel and perpendicular

m1=m2m_1 = m_2m1​=m2​m1m2=−1m_1 m_2 = -1m1​m2​=−1

Symbols: m1m_1m1​, m2m_2m2​: the slopes of the two lines.

The idea

Parallel lines rise at the same rate: equal slopes. Perpendicular lines have slopes that multiply to −1-1−1: flip the slope and change its sign (2→−122 \to -\tfrac122→−21​).

Worked example

Perpendicular to y=2x+1y = 2x + 1y=2x+1 through (2,1)(2, 1)(2,1): slope −12-\tfrac12−21​, so y−1=−12(x−2)y - 1 = -\tfrac12(x - 2)y−1=−21​(x−2), y=−x2+2y = -\tfrac x2 + 2y=−2x​+2 (yellow).

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Angle between two lines

tan⁡θ=∣m2−m11+m1m2∣\tan\theta = \left|\frac{m_2 - m_1}{1 + m_1 m_2}\right|tanθ=​1+m1​m2​m2​−m1​​​

Symbols: m1m_1m1​, m2m_2m2​: the slopes; θ\thetaθ: the acute angle between the lines.

The idea

Each slope is the tangent of an inclination angle; the angle between the lines is the difference of those angles, and the tangent subtraction formula gives this expression. The absolute value picks the acute angle. If 1+m1m2=01 + m_1 m_2 = 01+m1​m2​=0 the lines are perpendicular.

Worked example

y=xy = xy=x and y=3xy = 3xy=3x: tan⁡θ=3−11+3=12\tan\theta = \tfrac{3 - 1}{1 + 3} = \tfrac12tanθ=1+33−1​=21​, so θ≈26.6°\theta \approx 26.6°θ≈26.6°.

Point to line

d=∣Ax0+By0+C∣A2+B2d = \frac{|Ax_0 + By_0 + C|}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2}}d=A2+B2​∣Ax0​+By0​+C∣​

Symbols: (x0,y0)(x_0, y_0)(x0​,y0​): the point; Ax+By+C=0Ax + By + C = 0Ax+By+C=0: the line.

The idea

The shortest way from a point to a line is along the perpendicular. The formula plugs the point into the line’s general equation — that gives 0 only for points on the line — and divides by A2+B2\sqrt{A^2 + B^2}A2+B2​, the length of the normal vector.

Worked example

(1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) to 3x+4y−1=03x + 4y - 1 = 03x+4y−1=0: ∣3+8−1∣5=105=2\tfrac{\lvert 3 + 8 - 1\rvert}{5} = \tfrac{10}{5} = 25∣3+8−1∣​=510​=2.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Parallel lines

d=∣C1−C2∣A2+B2d = \frac{|C_1 - C_2|}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2}}d=A2+B2​∣C1​−C2​∣​

Symbols: The lines Ax+By+C1=0Ax + By + C_1 = 0Ax+By+C1​=0 and Ax+By+C2=0Ax + By + C_2 = 0Ax+By+C2​=0 (same AAA, BBB).

The idea

Write both lines with the same AAA and BBB (multiply one if needed). Then the distance is the gap between the constants divided by the length of the normal vector.

Worked example

3x+4y−2=03x + 4y - 2 = 03x+4y−2=0 and 3x+4y+8=03x + 4y + 8 = 03x+4y+8=0: d=∣−2−8∣5=2d = \tfrac{\lvert -2 - 8\rvert}{5} = 2d=5∣−2−8∣​=2.

Circles

Centre and radius

(x−a)2+(y−b)2=r2(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2(x−a)2+(y−b)2=r2

Symbols: (a,b)(a, b)(a,b): the centre, rrr: the radius.

The idea

A circle is every point at distance rrr from the centre (a,b)(a, b)(a,b). Write that distance with the distance formula and square it: that is the equation. Watch the signs: (y+1)2(y + 1)^2(y+1)2 means b=−1b = -1b=−1.

Worked example

(x−2)2+(y+1)2=9(x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 9(x−2)2+(y+1)2=9: centre (2,−1)(2, -1)(2,−1), radius 9=3\sqrt 9 = 39​=3.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

General form

x2+y2+Dx+Ey+F=0x^2 + y^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0x2+y2+Dx+Ey+F=0

Centre (−D2,−E2)\left(-\tfrac D2, -\tfrac E2\right)(−2D​,−2E​), r2=D2+E24−Fr^2 = \tfrac{D^2 + E^2}{4} - Fr2=4D2+E2​−F.

The idea

Expanding the squares gives x2+y2+Dx+Ey+F=0x^2 + y^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0x2+y2+Dx+Ey+F=0. To go back, complete the square in xxx and in yyy: the centre is (−D2,−E2)\left(-\tfrac D2, -\tfrac E2\right)(−2D​,−2E​) and r2=D2+E24−Fr^2 = \tfrac{D^2 + E^2}{4} - Fr2=4D2+E2​−F — if that is negative there is no circle.

Worked example

x2+y2−6x+4y−3=0x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y - 3 = 0x2+y2−6x+4y−3=0: (x−3)2−9+(y+2)2−4−3=0(x - 3)^2 - 9 + (y + 2)^2 - 4 - 3 = 0(x−3)2−9+(y+2)2−4−3=0, so (x−3)2+(y+2)2=16(x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 16(x−3)2+(y+2)2=16: centre (3,−2)(3, -2)(3,−2), radius 4.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Tangent at a point

(x0−a)(x−a)+(y0−b)(y−b)=r2(x_0 - a)(x - a) + (y_0 - b)(y - b) = r^2(x0​−a)(x−a)+(y0​−b)(y−b)=r2

Symbols: (x0,y0)(x_0, y_0)(x0​,y0​): the point of contact on the circle; (a,b)(a, b)(a,b): centre, rrr: radius.

The idea

The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. The formula comes from “doubling”: replace one factor of each square by the point’s coordinates. For a circle centred at the origin it is simply x0x+y0y=r2x_0x + y_0y = r^2x0​x+y0​y=r2.

Worked example

x2+y2=25x^2 + y^2 = 25x2+y2=25 at (3,4)(3, 4)(3,4): 3x+4y=253x + 4y = 253x+4y=25, i.e. y=25−3x4y = \tfrac{25 - 3x}{4}y=425−3x​. Its slope −34-\tfrac34−43​ is perpendicular to the radius slope 43\tfrac4334​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Line and circle

d<r: 2d < r:\ 2d<r: 2d=r: 1d = r:\ 1d=r: 1d>r: 0d > r:\ 0d>r: 0

ddd = distance from the centre to the line; the number of common points.

The idea

Compare the distance ddd from the centre to the line with the radius: closer than rrr — the line cuts the circle twice; exactly rrr — it touches (tangent); farther — it misses. This avoids solving the system.

Worked example

y=x+1y = x + 1y=x+1 and x2+y2=4x^2 + y^2 = 4x2+y2=4: d=∣1∣2≈0.71<2d = \tfrac{\lvert 1\rvert}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.71 < 2d=2​∣1∣​≈0.71<2, so 2 intersection points (blue line).

Ellipse

Equation

x2a2+y2b2=1\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1a2x2​+b2y2​=1(a>b>0)(a > b > 0)(a>b>0)

Symbols: aaa: the semi-major axis (half the long axis), bbb: the semi-minor axis.

The idea

A circle stretched in one direction. It crosses the xxx-axis at ±a\pm a±a and the yyy-axis at ±b\pm b±b; with a>ba > ba>b the long (major) axis is horizontal and has length 2a2a2a.

Worked example

x225+y29=1\tfrac{x^2}{25} + \tfrac{y^2}{9} = 125x2​+9y2​=1: a=5a = 5a=5, b=3b = 3b=3. Vertices (±5,0)(\pm 5, 0)(±5,0) and (0,±3)(0, \pm 3)(0,±3); the major axis has length 10.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Foci

F1,2=(±c,0)F_{1,2} = (\pm c, 0)F1,2​=(±c,0)c2=a2−b2c^2 = a^2 - b^2c2=a2−b2

Symbols: F1F_1F1​, F2F_2F2​: the foci; ccc: the distance from the centre to each focus.

The idea

The two foci lie on the major axis at (±c,0)(\pm c, 0)(±c,0), with c2=a2−b2c^2 = a^2 - b^2c2=a2−b2. Picture the right triangle from the centre to a focus and up to the end of the minor axis: its hypotenuse is aaa.

Worked example

a=5a = 5a=5, b=3b = 3b=3: c2=25−9=16c^2 = 25 - 9 = 16c2=25−9=16, c=4c = 4c=4, foci (±4,0)(\pm 4, 0)(±4,0). The pink segment from a focus to (0,3)(0, 3)(0,3) has length a=5a = 5a=5.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Definition

PF1+PF2=2aPF_1 + PF_2 = 2aPF1​+PF2​=2a

Symbols: PPP: any point of the ellipse; PF1PF_1PF1​, PF2PF_2PF2​: its distances to the two foci.

The idea

An ellipse is the set of points whose distances to the two foci add up to a constant 2a2a2a — the gardener’s construction with two pins and a loop of string. So if you know one focal distance, the other is 2a2a2a minus it.

Worked example

For x225+y29=1\tfrac{x^2}{25} + \tfrac{y^2}{9} = 125x2​+9y2​=1 the sum is 2a=102a = 102a=10. At P(3,2.4)P(3, 2.4)P(3,2.4): PF1=7.4PF_1 = 7.4PF1​=7.4 and PF2=2.6PF_2 = 2.6PF2​=2.6, which add to 10.

Eccentricity

e=ca<1e = \frac ca < 1e=ac​<1

Symbols: eee: the eccentricity, how flat the curve is (0 is a circle).

The idea

e=cae = \tfrac cae=ac​ measures how flat the ellipse is: e=0e = 0e=0 is a circle (foci at the centre), eee close to 1 is a long thin ellipse. Planet orbits have small eee (Earth: 0.017).

Worked example

x225+y29=1\tfrac{x^2}{25} + \tfrac{y^2}{9} = 125x2​+9y2​=1: c=4c = 4c=4, e=45=0.8e = \tfrac45 = 0.8e=54​=0.8 — quite flat.

Area and parametrisation

S=πabS = \pi abS=πab(acos⁡t, bsin⁡t)(a\cos t,\ b\sin t)(acost, bsint)

Symbols: SSS: the area; ttt: a parameter (an angle) that runs through [0,2π)[0, 2\pi)[0,2π).

The idea

Stretch the unit circle by aaa horizontally and bbb vertically: the point (cos⁡t,sin⁡t)(\cos t, \sin t)(cost,sint) goes to (acos⁡t,bsin⁡t)(a\cos t, b\sin t)(acost,bsint), and the area π\piπ is multiplied by ababab.

Worked example

x225+y29=1\tfrac{x^2}{25} + \tfrac{y^2}{9} = 125x2​+9y2​=1 has area 15π≈47.115\pi \approx 47.115π≈47.1. At t=60°t = 60°t=60° the point is (5⋅12,3⋅32)≈(2.5,2.6)(5\cdot\tfrac12, 3\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}) \approx (2.5, 2.6)(5⋅21​,3⋅23​​)≈(2.5,2.6).

Parabola

Equations

x2=4pyx^2 = 4pyx2=4pyy2=4pxy^2 = 4pxy2=4px

Focus (0,p)(0, p)(0,p), directrix y=−py = -py=−p (first form).

Symbols: ppp: the distance from the vertex to the focus.

The idea

x2=4pyx^2 = 4pyx2=4py opens upwards with focus (0,p)(0, p)(0,p) and directrix y=−py = -py=−p; y2=4pxy^2 = 4pxy2=4px opens to the right with focus (p,0)(p, 0)(p,0) and directrix x=−px = -px=−p. Read ppp by dividing the coefficient by 4.

Worked example

x2=8yx^2 = 8yx2=8y: 4p=84p = 84p=8, p=2p = 2p=2, focus (0,2)(0, 2)(0,2), directrix y=−2y = -2y=−2.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Definition

PF=d(P,ℓ)PF = d(P, \ell)PF=d(P,ℓ)

Every point is as far from the focus as from the directrix ℓ\ellℓ.

Symbols: PPP: a point of the parabola, FFF: the focus, d(P,ℓ)d(P, \ell)d(P,ℓ): the distance from PPP to the line ℓ\ellℓ.

The idea

Every point of a parabola is as far from the focus as from the directrix. So the distance to the focus is easy: for y2=4pxy^2 = 4pxy2=4px it is the horizontal distance to the line x=−px = -px=−p, i.e. x+px + px+p.

Worked example

y2=8xy^2 = 8xy2=8x (p=2p = 2p=2), point with x=3x = 3x=3: PF=3+2=5PF = 3 + 2 = 5PF=3+2=5 — no square roots needed.

Vertex form

y=a(x−h)2+ky = a(x - h)^2 + ky=a(x−h)2+k

Vertex (h,k)(h, k)(h,k), focus (h,k+14a)\left(h, k + \tfrac{1}{4a}\right)(h,k+4a1​).

The idea

Complete the square to turn ax2+bx+cax^2 + bx + cax2+bx+c into a(x−h)2+ka(x - h)^2 + ka(x−h)2+k; the vertex is (h,k)(h, k)(h,k) and h=−b2ah = -\tfrac{b}{2a}h=−2ab​. Then 1a=4p\tfrac1a = 4pa1​=4p gives the focus, ppp above the vertex when a>0a > 0a>0.

Worked example

y=2x2−8x+5=2(x2−4x+4)−8+5=2(x−2)2−3y = 2x^2 - 8x + 5 = 2(x^2 - 4x + 4) - 8 + 5 = 2(x - 2)^2 - 3y=2x2−8x+5=2(x2−4x+4)−8+5=2(x−2)2−3: vertex (2,−3)(2, -3)(2,−3).

Eccentricity

e=1e = 1e=1

Symbols: eee: the eccentricity; every parabola has e=1e = 1e=1.

The idea

For every parabola PFPFPF equals the distance to the directrix, so the ratio is exactly e=1e = 1e=1 — between the ellipse (e<1e < 1e<1) and the hyperbola (e>1e > 1e>1). All parabolas have the same shape; only the size ppp changes.

Worked example

y2=4pxy^2 = 4pxy2=4px through (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2): 4=4p4 = 4p4=4p, so p=1p = 1p=1, focus (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0).

Hyperbola

Equation

x2a2−y2b2=1\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1a2x2​−b2y2​=1

Symbols: aaa: distance from the centre to each vertex (±a,0)(\pm a, 0)(±a,0); bbb sets the slope of the asymptotes.

The idea

Same shape of equation as the ellipse but with a minus sign. It has two branches crossing the xxx-axis at ±a\pm a±a and never meets the yyy-axis; the distance between the vertices is 2a2a2a.

Worked example

x29−y216=1\tfrac{x^2}{9} - \tfrac{y^2}{16} = 19x2​−16y2​=1: a=3a = 3a=3, vertices (±3,0)(\pm 3, 0)(±3,0). At x=0x = 0x=0: −y216=1-\tfrac{y^2}{16} = 1−16y2​=1 has no solution, so no yyy-intercept.

Foci

F1,2=(±c,0)F_{1,2} = (\pm c, 0)F1,2​=(±c,0)c2=a2+b2c^2 = a^2 + b^2c2=a2+b2

Symbols: ccc: the distance from the centre to each focus.

The idea

The foci are outside the vertices at (±c,0)(\pm c, 0)(±c,0), and now the squares add: c2=a2+b2c^2 = a^2 + b^2c2=a2+b2. Compare the ellipse, where they subtract.

Worked example

a=3a = 3a=3, b=4b = 4b=4: c=9+16=5c = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5c=9+16​=5, foci (±5,0)(\pm 5, 0)(±5,0).

Definition

∣PF1−PF2∣=2a|PF_1 - PF_2| = 2a∣PF1​−PF2​∣=2a

Symbols: PPP: any point of the hyperbola; F1F_1F1​, F2F_2F2​: the foci.

The idea

A hyperbola is the set of points whose distances to the two foci differ by the constant 2a2a2a. On the right branch PF1−PF2=2aPF_1 - PF_2 = 2aPF1​−PF2​=2a, on the left branch the other way round — so one focal distance gives two possibilities for the other.

Worked example

x29−y216=1\tfrac{x^2}{9} - \tfrac{y^2}{16} = 19x2​−16y2​=1: 2a=62a = 62a=6. At P(5,163)P(5, \tfrac{16}{3})P(5,316​): PF2=163PF_2 = \tfrac{16}{3}PF2​=316​ and PF1=343PF_1 = \tfrac{34}{3}PF1​=334​, difference 6.

Asymptotes

y=±ba xy = \pm\frac ba\,xy=±ab​x

The idea

Far from the centre the 1 on the right becomes negligible, so x2a2≈y2b2\tfrac{x^2}{a^2} \approx \tfrac{y^2}{b^2}a2x2​≈b2y2​, i.e. y≈±baxy \approx \pm\tfrac ba xy≈±ab​x. The two asymptotes are the diagonals of the 2a×2b2a \times 2b2a×2b box around the centre.

Worked example

x29−y216=1\tfrac{x^2}{9} - \tfrac{y^2}{16} = 19x2​−16y2​=1: asymptotes y=±43xy = \pm\tfrac43 xy=±34​x, the diagonals of the 6×86 \times 86×8 box.

Eccentricity

e=ca>1e = \frac ca > 1e=ac​>1

The idea

e=cae = \tfrac cae=ac​ is now larger than 1 since c>ac > ac>a. The larger eee, the more open the branches (steeper asymptotes, ba=e2−1\tfrac ba = \sqrt{e^2 - 1}ab​=e2−1​).

Worked example

x29−y216=1\tfrac{x^2}{9} - \tfrac{y^2}{16} = 19x2​−16y2​=1: e=53≈1.67e = \tfrac53 \approx 1.67e=35​≈1.67.

Rectangular hyperbola

xy=kxy = kxy=k

Symbols: kkk: a non-zero constant; the asymptotes are the axes.

The idea

When a=ba = ba=b the asymptotes are perpendicular. Turned by 45° such a hyperbola becomes xy=kxy = kxy=k: the axes themselves are the asymptotes. y=kxy = \tfrac kxy=xk​ describes inverse proportion.

Worked example

xy=4xy = 4xy=4: vertices (2,2)(2, 2)(2,2) and (−2,−2)(-2, -2)(−2,−2) on the line y=xy = xy=x; as xxx doubles, yyy halves.

Tangents and chords of conics

Ellipse tangent at (x₀, y₀)

xx0a2+yy0b2=1\frac{x x_0}{a^2} + \frac{y y_0}{b^2} = 1a2xx0​​+b2yy0​​=1

Symbols: (x0,y0)(x_0, y_0)(x0​,y0​): the point of contact on the curve.

The idea

The same “doubling” rule as for the circle: replace x2x^2x2 by xx0x x_0xx0​ and y2y^2y2 by yy0y y_0yy0​. The point must lie on the ellipse for this to be a tangent.

Worked example

x225+y29=1\tfrac{x^2}{25} + \tfrac{y^2}{9} = 125x2​+9y2​=1 at (4,95)(4, \tfrac95)(4,59​): 4x25+y5=1\tfrac{4x}{25} + \tfrac{y}{5} = 1254x​+5y​=1, i.e. y=5−45xy = 5 - \tfrac45 xy=5−54​x.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Hyperbola tangent at (x₀, y₀)

xx0a2−yy0b2=1\frac{x x_0}{a^2} - \frac{y y_0}{b^2} = 1a2xx0​​−b2yy0​​=1

The idea

Again double the variables: x2→xx0x^2 \to x x_0x2→xx0​, y2→yy0y^2 \to y y_0y2→yy0​, keeping the minus sign. The tangent at a vertex is vertical; far out it approaches an asymptote.

Worked example

x29−y216=1\tfrac{x^2}{9} - \tfrac{y^2}{16} = 19x2​−16y2​=1 at (5,163)(5, \tfrac{16}{3})(5,316​): 5x9−y3=1\tfrac{5x}{9} - \tfrac{y}{3} = 195x​−3y​=1, i.e. y=53x−3y = \tfrac53 x - 3y=35​x−3.

Parabola tangent at (x₀, y₀)

y2=4px:  yy0=2p(x+x0)y^2 = 4px:\ \ y y_0 = 2p(x + x_0)y2=4px:  yy0​=2p(x+x0​)x2=4py:  xx0=2p(y+y0)x^2 = 4py:\ \ x x_0 = 2p(y + y_0)x2=4py:  xx0​=2p(y+y0​)

The idea

Doubling for a parabola: y2→yy0y^2 \to y y_0y2→yy0​ and the linear term x→x+x02x \to \tfrac{x + x_0}{2}x→2x+x0​​. For y2=4pxy^2 = 4pxy2=4px that gives yy0=2p(x+x0)y y_0 = 2p(x + x_0)yy0​=2p(x+x0​).

Worked example

y2=8xy^2 = 8xy2=8x (p=2p = 2p=2) at (2,4)(2, 4)(2,4): 4y=4(x+2)4y = 4(x + 2)4y=4(x+2), i.e. y=x+2y = x + 2y=x+2. It meets the axis at x=−2x = -2x=−2: the tangent at (x0,y0)(x_0, y_0)(x0​,y0​) always crosses the axis at −x0-x_0−x0​.

Tangency condition

y=mx+c:c2=a2m2+b2y = mx + c:\quad c^2 = a^2m^2 + b^2y=mx+c:c2=a2m2+b2

For the ellipse; hyperbola: c2=a2m2−b2c^2 = a^2m^2 - b^2c2=a2m2−b2; parabola y2=4pxy^2 = 4pxy2=4px: c=pmc = \tfrac pmc=mp​. In general substitute and set Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0.

Symbols: mmm: the slope and ccc: the yyy-intercept of the line.

The idea

Substitute y=mx+cy = mx + cy=mx+c into the ellipse: you get a quadratic in xxx. The line is tangent when that quadratic has a double root (discriminant 0), which simplifies to c2=a2m2+b2c^2 = a^2m^2 + b^2c2=a2m2+b2. For a given slope there are two tangents, c=±a2m2+b2c = \pm\sqrt{a^2m^2 + b^2}c=±a2m2+b2​.

Worked example

x24+y2=1\tfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 14x2​+y2=1 with slope 1: c2=4+1=5c^2 = 4 + 1 = 5c2=4+1=5, so y=x±5y = x \pm\sqrt5y=x±5​ — the two blue lines.

Latus rectum

2b2a  (E,H)\frac{2b^2}{a}\ \ (E, H)a2b2​  (E,H)4p  (y2=4px)4p \ \ (y^2 = 4px)4p  (y2=4px)

Chord through a focus, perpendicular to the main axis. E: ellipse, H: hyperbola.

The idea

The latus rectum is the chord through a focus perpendicular to the major axis. Put x=cx = cx=c into the equation: y=±b2ay = \pm\tfrac{b^2}{a}y=±ab2​, so its length is 2b2a\tfrac{2b^2}{a}a2b2​ for the ellipse and the hyperbola; for y2=4pxy^2 = 4pxy2=4px, x=px = px=p gives y=±2py = \pm 2py=±2p, length 4p4p4p.

Worked example

x225+y29=1\tfrac{x^2}{25} + \tfrac{y^2}{9} = 125x2​+9y2​=1: 2⋅95=3.6\tfrac{2\cdot 9}{5} = 3.652⋅9​=3.6 — the pink chord from (4,−1.8)(4, -1.8)(4,−1.8) to (4,1.8)(4, 1.8)(4,1.8).

Focal chord of a parabola

y2=4px:  ∣AB∣=x1+x2+2py^2 = 4px:\ \ |AB| = x_1 + x_2 + 2py2=4px:  ∣AB∣=x1​+x2​+2pPF=x0+pPF = x_0 + pPF=x0​+p

Symbols: A(x1,y1)A(x_1, y_1)A(x1​,y1​), B(x2,y2)B(x_2, y_2)B(x2​,y2​): the ends of a chord through the focus; P(x0,y0)P(x_0, y_0)P(x0​,y0​): a point of the parabola.

The idea

By the definition, each endpoint’s distance to the focus is its distance to the directrix, x+px + px+p. A chord through the focus is made of two such pieces, so its length is x1+x2+2px_1 + x_2 + 2px1​+x2​+2p — just add.

Worked example

y2=8xy^2 = 8xy2=8x (p=2p = 2p=2), focal chord with endpoints at x=1x = 1x=1 and x=4x = 4x=4: ∣AB∣=1+4+4=9\lvert AB\rvert = 1 + 4 + 4 = 9∣AB∣=1+4+4=9.

Focal distances of an ellipse

PF1=a+e x0PF_1 = a + e\,x_0PF1​=a+ex0​PF2=a−e x0PF_2 = a - e\,x_0PF2​=a−ex0​

Symbols: P(x0,y0)P(x_0, y_0)P(x0​,y0​): a point of the ellipse, eee: the eccentricity.

The idea

For a point of the ellipse with abscissa x0x_0x0​, the distances to the foci are linear in x0x_0x0​: a+ex0a + e x_0a+ex0​ to the left focus and a−ex0a - e x_0a−ex0​ to the right one. They add to 2a2a2a, as the definition demands.

Worked example

a=5a = 5a=5, e=0.8e = 0.8e=0.8, x0=3x_0 = 3x0​=3: PF1=5+2.4=7.4PF_1 = 5 + 2.4 = 7.4PF1​=5+2.4=7.4, PF2=5−2.4=2.6PF_2 = 5 - 2.4 = 2.6PF2​=5−2.4=2.6 — the same as computed with the distance formula.

Chord with a given midpoint

mAB=−b2x0a2y0m_{AB} = -\frac{b^2 x_0}{a^2 y_0}mAB​=−a2y0​b2x0​​

Ellipse chord with midpoint (x0,y0)(x_0, y_0)(x0​,y0​) (difference of the two equations).

Symbols: mABm_{AB}mAB​: the slope of the chord ABABAB.

The idea

Write the ellipse equation for both endpoints and subtract: the differences factor as (x1−x2)(x1+x2)(x_1 - x_2)(x_1 + x_2)(x1​−x2​)(x1​+x2​), and x1+x2=2x0x_1 + x_2 = 2x_0x1​+x2​=2x0​. Dividing gives the slope of the chord in terms of the midpoint alone (the “point difference” method).

Worked example

x216+y29=1\tfrac{x^2}{16} + \tfrac{y^2}{9} = 116x2​+9y2​=1, midpoint (2,1)(2, 1)(2,1): m=−9⋅216⋅1=−98m = -\tfrac{9\cdot 2}{16\cdot 1} = -\tfrac98m=−16⋅19⋅2​=−89​, so the chord is y−1=−98(x−2)y - 1 = -\tfrac98(x - 2)y−1=−89​(x−2).

Conics in general

Classification

Ax2+Bxy+Cy2+Dx+Ey+F=0Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0Ax2+Bxy+Cy2+Dx+Ey+F=0

B2−4AC<0B^2 - 4AC < 0B2−4AC<0 ellipse, =0= 0=0 parabola, >0> 0>0 hyperbola.

Symbols: A,B,C,D,E,FA, B, C, D, E, FA,B,C,D,E,F: the coefficients of the equation.

The idea

The quadratic part Ax2+Bxy+Cy2Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2Ax2+Bxy+Cy2 decides the type through B2−4ACB^2 - 4ACB2−4AC: negative — ellipse (or circle); zero — parabola; positive — hyperbola. The linear terms only move the curve. (Degenerate cases — a point, two lines, nothing — can also occur.)

Worked example

x2+xy+y2=3x^2 + xy + y^2 = 3x2+xy+y2=3: B2−4AC=1−4=−3<0B^2 - 4AC = 1 - 4 = -3 < 0B2−4AC=1−4=−3<0, an ellipse tilted at 45°.

Focus–directrix

PFd(P,ℓ)=e\frac{PF}{d(P, \ell)} = ed(P,ℓ)PF​=e

e<1e < 1e<1 ellipse, e=1e = 1e=1 parabola, e>1e > 1e>1 hyperbola.

Symbols: FFF: the focus, ℓ\ellℓ: the directrix (a line), eee: the eccentricity.

The idea

Every conic (except the circle) is the set of points whose distance to a focus is eee times the distance to a line, the directrix. e<1e < 1e<1 gives an ellipse, e=1e = 1e=1 a parabola, e>1e > 1e>1 a hyperbola — one definition for all three.

Worked example

Focus at the origin, directrix x=4x = 4x=4: with e=12e = \tfrac12e=21​ you get the blue ellipse, with e=1e = 1e=1 the yellow parabola. A point at distance 6 from the directrix of an e=12e = \tfrac12e=21​ conic is 3 from the focus.

Polar form

r=e p1+ecos⁡θr = \frac{e\,p}{1 + e\cos\theta}r=1+ecosθep​

Symbols: rrr: distance from the focus, θ\thetaθ: polar angle, eee: eccentricity, ppp: distance from the focus to the directrix.

The idea

With the focus at the pole and the directrix at distance ppp, the focus–directrix definition becomes r=ep1+ecos⁡θr = \tfrac{ep}{1 + e\cos\theta}r=1+ecosθep​. This is how orbits are written: rrr is smallest at θ=0\theta = 0θ=0 (perihelion) and largest at θ=π\theta = \piθ=π when e<1e < 1e<1.

Worked example

r=61+0.5cos⁡θr = \tfrac{6}{1 + 0.5\cos\theta}r=1+0.5cosθ6​: e=0.5e = 0.5e=0.5, an ellipse. At θ=0\theta = 0θ=0: r=4r = 4r=4; at θ=π\theta = \piθ=π: r=60.5=12r = \tfrac{6}{0.5} = 12r=0.56​=12.
